title: Interface and accessibility
thesis: A roguelike's depth should live in its systems, not in the effort it takes to operate them: the talks converge on few contextual commands, automation of no-brainer decisions, previews and on-demand explanation, and interfaces designed for newcomers first with power tools layered on. Accessibility, whether for blind players, children or people who never learned ASCII, is reached by testing with the players you are not, and the genre's text heritage makes it unusually achievable.

sections.heading: The interface is the design: why roguelike UI decides who can play
sections.brief: Open with the argument that interface quality is a design problem, not polish layered on afterwards. Lead with Angband's ergonomic changes (approachable without being easier, eeSk665OXkM#6) and Subset Games' finding that Into the Breach's painful playtests were a presentation failure, not a design failure, with half or more of development going to UX (rNi5nO5yqLs#2). Then stage the central warning: Thomas Biskup's account of ADOM's 'slick' UI being condemned on Steam and his claim that power-user communities are the biggest obstacle to mainstream interfaces (hnoF_bL-HjI#1, #2, PTIsUSbQ0TA#2, iZUXjbcAfYs#3); set this beside the convergent views of Zapata, Slashie and Josh Ge that the bar has risen and that importing conveniences from non-roguelikes reaches far more players (wwc7pZqs9UA#9, R8DSq8qSJ44@32392#2, jviNpRGuCIU#19, 9se2M27LuOs#11, KYlq0Msu6hc#1). Counterweights: conventions are sticky (Sable, 6ohPU0sECFE#6) and ADOM promised veterans no more relearning (iZUXjbcAfYs#4); polish can excuse slowness (Bond) and UI is 'pick your poison' (Furmanski). End with guidance: treat UX as a budget line from day one, distrust feedback that comes only from veterans, and keep 'what would the clearest classic roguelike UI look like?' (rNi5nO5yqLs#10) as the open goal.

sections.heading: Simple surface, deep game: commands, options and detail levels
sections.brief: Argue that depth belongs in the game logic, not in the number of keys: Biskup's 'hide the complexity on the UI side' (hnoF_bL-HjI#6), Ultimate ADOM's seven keys versus ADOM's 100+ commands (hnoF_bL-HjI#4) and its mobile-first, controller-first design with power tools added later (iZUXjbcAfYs#25). Show the strong convergence on contextual action through movement: Slashie and Santiago Zapata's Rodney (movement plus one button, wall-jump on bump), George Moromisato on NetHack's bump-to-attack core with rare verbs revealed as needed, Brogue's stairs used by stepping onto them, Rogue's items needing no further input, Egart's rituals that refuse menus, and Nick Bush borrowing intuitive platform controls (R8DSq8qSJ44@32392#3, TMxzVy7-VYQ#13, QBZkvtGucBU#7, Uo9-IcHhq_w#11, X4be22WoVgg#8, q4Tf0vf2kiI#3, R8DSq8qSJ44@1660#0). Then the input-device question: Cogmind's data that keyboard players are a minority, so everything must be mouse-reachable (9se2M27LuOs#10), touch from the start for mobile (TMxzVy7-VYQ#14), the ADOM fan who never knew he could drink potions (hnoF_bL-HjI#3), and hjkl's origin as a hardware accident (6ohPU0sECFE#2). Then options and detail levels: Biskup's 'every option has a price' (hnoF_bL-HjI#5) against Ultimate ADOM's switchable detail levels and the dice-notation finding (hnoF_bL-HjI#14, #9, PTIsUSbQ0TA#16), plus Berman's small-number arithmetic, data-driven tooltips and per-platform rule variants. Multiplayer designers (Plummer's HVNTRS and Scrubbin' Trubble) reached the same rules for a different reason, keeping turns fast. End with practical rules: one core verb, contextual triggers, mouse/touch parity, few visible options with good defaults, detail levels designed in from the start.

sections.heading: Respecting the player's time: speed, automation and tedium
sections.brief: Start from Jeremiah Reid's one hard rule, that animations must never block a player from acting as fast as they want, and his technique of applying every input immediately and speeding pending animations (xSYVQc7cH-4#6, #12); contrast Thomas Robertson's case that super attacks may legitimately halt play if they are skippable (f1t4yPjfZyM#2). Then automation of no-brainer decisions: Cogmind's part-swap key and auto-labels, DCSS's auto-explore born from player-submitted fixes, Angband's fire-at-nearest (9se2M27LuOs#13, #12, tg-CjNodlmY#2, eeSk665OXkM#8), with click-to-travel in Forska. Use the Dwarf Fortress origin story (Mutant Miner's click-click slog) and the MIT Mystery Hunt ten-second turns as cautionary tales of tedium and latency. Then stage the disagreement: auto-travel is controversial and HyperRogue deliberately omits it (wOlSws-OI2o#4); Pichlmair and Zhou argue that physical execution and memorised commands are part of the fun and simplifying them can strip energy (EMb6B2cIJps#12, KRZHT-gktD0#7); Vagante's unpaused inventory makes menu time a risk on purpose. End with guidance: automate decisions with one right answer, keep automation optional, and never make the player wait on the presentation.

sections.heading: Making consequences visible: previews, tooltips and threat display
sections.brief: Frame with Joseph Hewitt's magician's principle that UI design is directing attention, or players miss required mechanics (dCWWId16VAo#1). The core convergence is on showing outcomes before commitment: Monster Train's damage previews, Brian Cronin's black-box-sim previews from a copied world state, Desktop Dungeons' combat prediction and Danny Day's regret about not having copyable state, Rift Wizard's unsafe-tile overlay (qO3CIpP62Q0#4, jhcHlg7YhPg#11, p48ArjJweSo#9, VVRomN99Ygw#13); give the implementation detail. Then signalling stakes ahead of choices: Darren Grey's threat signals and Hades-style door iconography (C2sm-z7Ag4U#10, bpGRyzWCWwk#4), and feedback that must register fast (Lisa Brown on Rogue's combat text, Bloomquist adding damage messages). Then reminders on demand: Slay the Spire's instant tooltips, Tangledeep item cards separating function from flavour, everything on one screen (Berman, Dwarf Fortress's non-modal philosophy), Hearthstone's digitisation. Close with warnings where displays mislead or overwhelm: Grams' shadow markers read as one turn each, CK2's wall of trait icons, Thousand Hells losing the visible deck count, and Shattered Pixel Dungeon's icon-grid changelog as the fix for walls of text. End with a practical list: preview anything that can be simulated, signal danger before the choice, tooltips instantly, one screen where possible.

sections.heading: What the interface says: messages, labels and tone
sections.brief: Argue that every message, label and statistic carries authorial meaning beyond its information. Start with the message log itself: Ultimate ADOM moving effects out of text boxes and into the world (PTIsUSbQ0TA#9), Kingdom of Loathing's haiku mode, which may restyle text but must never hide game information (jNUMRG_tvrY#5), and the practical cost of good message text (Crawl's pluralisation code, GMkBT4UbvAs#6). Then tone as design: Caves of Qud's terse 'your mind is stranded here' (kvCky6BbTuE#12), Nathan Savant's UI as character state, Nauticrawl's diegetic cockpit monitors mapping HP, hunger and stamina onto hull, fuel and battery, Alexandra Leonhart's unreliable message-log narrator as unexplored space. Then what labels and stats tell players about how they are meant to play: Andrew Aversa's scale of permadeath option presentation and mode labels (kn2QkH5lByw#2, #3), Luck be a Landlord refusing a win-rate stat, Roundguard putting unlocks front and centre, NetHack declining to warn before breaking a conduct, and DCSS's morgue file as the game's closing statement on a run. Set Aversa's 'equitable listing' against designers who deliberately steer. End with guidance: decide what each label implies about the 'real' way to play, and never let style override legibility.

sections.heading: Windows onto the simulation: making deep systems legible
sections.brief: For simulation-heavy games the interface problem is not too many commands but too many events. Start with Max Kreminski's warning that Dwarf Fortress and Crusader Kings expose simulations through inscrutable UI and drown players in insignificant events, and his proposal to give players sense-making tools rather than simplify the simulation (BDcZSWHu8RQ#6); pair with Jasmine Otto's 'narrative instrument' for aiming attention (NjIDVIIg1lY#0). Then techniques: Jonathan Lessard's chronicles, a live hyperlinked wiki of the world (D8A9dpITLAU#2); Aaron Reed's argument for showing the seams of procedural text (x0Xh4oCX9t0#13); CK3's two-word epithets surfacing hidden AI stats; Caves of Qud's chronological journal; Banished Vault's delta-v map as heavy abstraction; Ultima Ratio Regum's searchable, colour-coded dialogue list; emoji for NPC relationship states; Synthesifter's authoring interface. Close with open problems: Rich Wilson's 'interaction articulation' (expressing intent like grief) and Scott Anderson on seeing into 3D falling-sand volumes. End with guidance: give players filters, histories and summaries of hidden state, and let them see what changed and why.

sections.heading: Letters, tiles and symbols: choosing a visual vocabulary
sections.brief: Set up the ASCII-versus-tiles question as a trade-off rather than a taste war. Lead with Joel Ryan's association/differentiation framework (ASCII glyphs classify and are easy to tell apart, tiles are easy to associate but hard to differentiate, UIsNv3UOzvA#7), then Evan Ovadia's steep-learning-curve point and his symbolic middle ground (Xwa1KbXqeGQ#1, #4, #5), and droqen's view that ASCII and numbers boil a game down to its mechanics (6Whz8bvjAKo#5). Then the imaginative case: Rogue's lab players screaming at a 'T', Leonard Richardson's imaginary play, Zapata's 'happy accident', Nick Montfort on defamiliarising the alphabet, Darren Grey's utilitarian aesthetic. Then practice: porting ASCII signals to tiles in Sil-Q, DCSS shipping both displays to widen appeal, NetHack's same-glyph decoys turning ambiguity into a mechanic, self-describing signs for ambiguous retro graphics, Sea of Rifts' top-down readability rules. End with text-as-graphics experiments (Furmanski's text-only 3D world and static images, La Horde du Contrevent's typographic layout and countdown pagination, Dragon's Descent losing text to cartridge limits) and guidance: choose the vocabulary for differentiation of threats, and if offering tiles, re-encode every signal the glyphs carried.

sections.heading: Building the display: terminals, fonts, grids and overlays
sections.brief: A technical section, specific enough to implement from. Start with the terminal heritage and its constraints: Ken Arnold repainting only Rogue's inventory window at 300 baud, the VT100's 80x24, and curses' optimised redraws turning to line noise on the wrong terminal (IaB7iQhts_c#7, 6ohPU0sECFE#3, tmrYfnMrifw#11). Then modern text-mode rendering: Patrick Devine's clear-update-redraw loop and Unicode quadrant characters (16 combinations, two colours per cell, font and line-spacing caveats; ckDp6p4HbqA#0, #3, #4, #5), Gabriel Santos's font aspect ratios (1:1 top-down, ~1:2 side view) and 20+ pixel-exact font sizes (5sFVVQcUWVE#4, #5), Joe Sondow's emoji grids with no matching whitespace (4byHHDeVKoA#3). Then the browser and odd substrates: Chris McCormick's HTML overlays and CSS-centred view, Sea of Rifts' SDF parchment panels, Trogue's darkness and fog layers in a tile-rewrite language, Google Sheets as a turn-based engine, Desktop Dungeons' swappable click handlers for input modes (p48ArjJweSo#7). Finish with geometry and view: HyperRogue's projections, one-dimensional dungeons placing UI on the spare axis, and line of sight being rare in roguelike platformers. Guidance: pick rendering technique by the information it must carry and test on the platforms that will display it.

sections.heading: Playing without seeing: blind and low-vision accessibility
sections.brief: This section rests almost entirely on Alexei Pepers' accessible NetHack research (2016 talk and 2018 Q&A), so say so plainly and organise it by problem rather than by talk. Open with the goal (accessible games that are as deep as sighted ones, e8Itfp3MHQ4#0) and the opportunity (ASCII roguelikes already deliver most information as text, e8Itfp3MHQ4#9). Then what the team built: the view command with exact tile offsets and the 'feel' cursor, feature lists with auto-travel, and the shared problem of positional movement (e8Itfp3MHQ4#4, #5, 5y_IAdOwaYs#12). Then the central open problem of conveying precise space in text without verbosity (e8Itfp3MHQ4#13, #11), the alternatives and their costs: raw screen-reading of ASCII, Crawl's auto-explore that disorients, Angband's lists for partial vision, text/audio roguelikes that drop the map and change combat, spatial audio as a partial aid, absolute coordinates as a suggestion. Then process lessons: no substitute for testing with visually impaired players (e8Itfp3MHQ4#6), emergent tactics like pet shop theft reveal gaps, make contested preferences options (e8Itfp3MHQ4#7), and accessibility helps everyone (e8Itfp3MHQ4#10). Close with later work: NetHack 3.6, BrogueSpeak, ARIA tags in The Fog, tab-navigable HTML overlays, Roguelike Radio's episode. End with a concrete checklist of features.

sections.heading: Testing for players unlike you: children, parents, newcomers and different minds
sections.brief: Argue that accessibility beyond vision is mostly a testing discipline: simulate the player you are not. Lead with Caelyn Sandel's point that recurring new-player questions mark accessibility gaps and that text-heavy help screens make people give up (NANqgqeqh2k#8, #1). The core is Michael Langford's toolkit for children and parents, which is unusually concrete: in-game button remapping, recording small hands on controllers and avoiding chorded held inputs, shaking a wrapped controller at menus and adding confirmations, fake-localising the font to simulate pre-literacy, sitting 1.5x further away to test text size, fixing deaths right after load screens, letting 'cheese' strategies work in co-op, and offering easy characters of different genders (wPN5bPxWXm8#1-#8). Then broaden: Hannah Blair Salzman on why roguelikes suit neurodivergent players, Playscii's pre-filled starting document as an on-ramp, and blekkenhorst's content warnings and lines-and-veils for immersive horror. End with a list of cheap tests a small team can run this week.

sections.heading: Beyond the keyboard: platforms, controllers and the player's body
sections.brief: The frontier section. Open with Yong Zhen Zhou's claim that redesigning the controller expands what the game is, and that input semantics change the player's role (puppeteer versus drill sergeant) (KRZHT-gktD0#0, #3); even on standard hardware, Slay the Spire's Shivs feel better flung on a phone (KRZHT-gktD0#6). Then concrete adaptations: Josh Grams' turn-based flight on gamepad (one key per direction, a move button to stop analog wiggles costing turns), Qristy Overton's Brogue on a dance pad (works because turns wait for input), Line Wobbler, Bad News staged with a live actor, and Julian Jarboe's exercise of imagining playback on cheap earbuds versus a home theatre. Then reach across platforms and networks: DCSS WebTiles and SSH servers, NAO's browser terminal, ADOM's 24+ platforms, and Leif Bloomquist's one shared world across C64, browser, telnet and mobile (three talks on the same project, 2018-2020: treat as one evolving case, not three). End with guidance: design input around the platform's natural gestures, check that turn-based waiting is preserved, and consider where and on what the game will actually be played.
